title_en: Huang Ying v. Meisheng Real Estate Company — dispute over commercial housing pre-sale contract
ruling_gist_en: With respect to obvious defects in the purchased house, the owner claimed to have clearly raised written objections on the Owner Occupancy Acceptance Form held by the developer. The developer refused to submit the Owner Occupancy Acceptance Form signed by the owner, but argued that the owner accepted the current condition of the house on the ground that the owner had already moved in. According to the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Litigation, it can be inferred that the owner's claim of having raised objections is established.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over pre-sale commercial housing contract; Second instance; Intermediate People's Court; Beijing Municipality; Natural person; Legal person; Contract Law; Determination of objections to housing defects; Elements of liability for breach of contract; Reversal of judgment; Pre-sale of commercial housing; Housing defects; Decorative steel beams; Contract dispute; Right to privacy; Real estate company pre-sale commercial housing contract dispute
full_text_en:
Huang Ying v. Beijing Meisheng Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Pre-sale Contract for Commercial Housing

【Ruling Summary】

Where an owner asserts that he/she has raised a written objection in the "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form" signed by the developer regarding an obvious defect in the purchased property, and the developer refuses to produce the "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form" bearing the owner's signature but claims that the owner has accepted the condition of the property by virtue of having taken occupancy, in accordance with Article 75 of the "Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings," it may be presumed that the owner's claim of having raised an objection is valid.

Pursuant to Article 107 of the Contract Law, where the delivered property does not conform to the specifications of the pre-sale contract for commercial housing, the developer shall bear liability for breach of contract to the owner. Any changes to the building features made at the time of delivery, regardless of whether they have been approved by administrative authorities or comply with building codes, pertain to a separate legal relationship and shall not constitute grounds for the developer to be exempted from liability for non-performance or breach of contract.

Plaintiff: Huang Ying, female, 35 years old, employee, residing at Hufang Road, Xuanwu District, Beijing.

Defendant: Beijing Meisheng Real Estate Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at Jiugong Town, Daxing District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Yang Meiling, General Manager of the Company.

Plaintiff Huang Ying filed an action with the Daxing District People's Court of Beijing against Defendant Beijing Meisheng Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Meisheng Real Estate Company) due to a dispute over a pre-sale contract for commercial housing.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The plaintiff purchased a property pre-sold by the defendant by entering into a contract. At the time of going through the occupancy procedures, the plaintiff discovered that there was a decorative steel beam outside the living room window of the property. This steel beam not only obstructed the window, causing visual and psychological distress to the plaintiff, but also threatened the plaintiff's personal and property safety as well as the right to privacy. During the process of concluding the contract between the plaintiff and the defendant, the defendant did not inform the plaintiff of the existence of this steel beam outside the window through the sand table model at the sales office, the model unit on display, or any other promotional materials, nor did it specify in the property purchase contract that there was a steel beam outside the window. The plaintiff repeatedly requested in writing that the defendant resolve this issue, but the defendant refused on various pretexts. The plaintiff prayed for an order that the defendant remove the decorative steel beam outside the plaintiff's window and bear the costs of this action.

Defendant's Defense: The defendant acknowledged that the steel beam outside the window as alleged by the plaintiff existed. This steel beam was installed in accordance with the overall design plan of the entire residential community approved by the relevant government departments, considering the aesthetics and coordination of the community, and it complies with building codes. The entire community is now completed and has passed inspection and acceptance. The plaintiff should consider the interests of the entire community. Moreover, the plaintiff has already taken occupancy, indicating that the plaintiff has accepted the current condition of the property. The defendant did not agree with the plaintiff's claims.

The Daxing District People's Court of Beijing found the following facts upon trial:

On August 17, 2003, Plaintiff Huang Ying and Defendant Meisheng Real Estate Company entered into a "Commercial Housing Sale Contract," stipulating: Huang Ying (the buyer) purchased from Meisheng Real Estate Company (the seller) one unit of pre-sold commercial housing, being Unit 502, Building 2, Section E-7 of Meiran·Beimei Taidu (also known as "Meili New World"), with a building area of 143.4 square meters, for a total price of RMB 567,864. On August 16, 2004, Meisheng Real Estate Company issued an "Occupancy Notice" to Huang Ying. Huang Ying has now completed the occupancy procedures and has paid the full purchase price for the property. In the same month, Huang Ying sent a letter to Meisheng Real Estate Company regarding the steel beam outside the window.

Separately, it was found that on June 30, 2003, in the construction drawings of Defendant Meisheng Real Estate Company approved by the Beijing Architectural Design and Research Institute, a decorative steel beam was designed outside the disputed property. On the sand table model displayed by Meisheng Real Estate Company for the pre-sale of the property, there was no decorative steel beam outside the disputed property. In the "Commercial Housing Sale Contract" signed by both parties, there was no provision regarding the existence of a steel beam outside the living room. The disputed property has now been accepted as completed, and the as-built drawings have also been reviewed and approved by the relevant government departments.

The above facts are confirmed by the statements of both parties, the "Commercial Housing Sale Contract," photographs of the sand table model, the Beijing construction project construction drawings, the design document review report, the as-built drawings, and other evidence.

The Daxing District People's Court of Beijing held:

The "Commercial Housing Sale Contract" signed by Plaintiff Huang Ying and Defendant Meisheng Real Estate Company represented the true intentions of both parties, its contents did not violate laws and regulations, and it should be confirmed as legal and valid. The sand table model displayed by Meisheng Real Estate Company for the pre-sale of the property could only reflect the general overview of the exterior of the entire community and could not reflect the various details of the building facilities. Therefore, the standards for the exterior walls and interior decoration of the pre-sold property should be based on the construction drawings, as-built drawings, and the stipulations in the "Commercial Housing Sale Contract" as approved by the relevant government departments. The as-built drawings approved by the relevant government departments showed that the design of the disputed property did not violate mandatory provisions of laws and regulations, and the construction complied with the corresponding building codes. At the time of handing over the property, Huang Ying did not raise any objections and actually completed the occupancy procedures. Now, on the grounds that the steel beam outside the window infringed upon her personal and property safety and right to privacy, and caused visual and psychological distress, she sought an order that Meisheng Real Estate Company remove the steel beam. As there was no contractual basis and no evidence of damage, her claim was not supported.

Accordingly, the Daxing District People's Court of Beijing rendered judgment on March 20, 2005:

Reject all claims of plaintiff Huang Ying.

Court costs of RMB 50 shall be borne by plaintiff Huang Ying.

Huang Ying, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, arguing: 1. This case is a contract dispute; both parties should act in accordance with the contract, and the court should also resolve the dispute in accordance with the contract. Since the first instance admitted that the contract did not address the existence or absence of a beam, it could not add clauses such as "review and approval by relevant government departments" to this issue not stipulated in the contract. 2. The appellant purchased a property under construction, not an existing property; therefore, she could only rely on promotional brochures and the sand table model to decide on entering into the property purchase contract. This was the fundamental reason why the contract did not mention the steel beam. Before the contract was signed, the appellee was clearly aware of the presence or absence of the steel beam but deliberately concealed this fact, thus breaching the contract first. Dismissing the appellant's claims on the ground that there was no contractual basis was a reversal of right and wrong. 3. Before occupancy, the appellee did not inform the appellant of the existence of the beam outside the property. At the time of occupancy, the appellant signed the "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form" only because she had no other choice, but she also raised a clear written objection on that form regarding the decorative steel beam outside the window. The finding of the first instance that the appellant did not raise any objection at the time of property handover was not factual. The appellant prayed: 1. To set aside the judgment of first instance; 2. To order the appellee to move the decorative crossbeam upward by 55 centimeters.

Meisheng Real Estate Company agreed with the judgment of first instance.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts upon trial:

The building number of the property purchased by Appellant Huang Ying had been changed from Unit 502, Building 2, Section E-7 as stated in the "Commercial Housing Sale Contract" to Unit 502, Building 2, Building 10. Regarding the steel beam outside the window of this unit, Huang Ying repeatedly stated in the first instance that she had raised a written objection through the "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form," which was kept by Appellee Meisheng Real Estate Company. During the second instance, upon request by the court, Meisheng Real Estate Company refused to produce the "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form" bearing Huang Ying's signature.

Upon on-site observation, the steel beam outside the window of the disputed property was purely a decorative feature of the building's exterior facade and had no impact on the main structure of the building. The crossbeam at the bottom of the decorative feature was located between the 5th and 6th floors, causing a certain degree of permanent obstruction to the windows of some units on the 5th floor, thereby affecting the visual experience of persons inside the rooms.

Otherwise, the second instance confirmed the other facts found in the first instance.

During the second instance, Appellant Huang Ying submitted a report issued by Beijing Capital Engineering Architectural Design Co., Ltd., which held a valid qualification certificate. The main content of the report was: To avoid affecting the lighting of residents on the 5th floor, including Huang Ying, Wang Yongqi, Wu Weibing, Han Junwei, Mo Li, Liu Yu, and Zhao Yuanzhao, it was recommended that the bottom crossbeam of the decorative steel beam outside the windows of the 5th floor units of the D-type unit in Meili New World be moved upward by 55 centimeters from its current position and re-welded. Upon examination, both parties had no objection to the above report of Beijing Capital Engineering Architectural Design Co., Ltd.

The issues in dispute in this case were: 1. Did Huang Ying accept the steel beam outside the window of the disputed property at the time of occupancy? 2. Did the existence of the steel beam constitute a breach of contract by Meisheng Real Estate Company? Should Meisheng Real Estate Company bear liability for breach of contract for this?

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held:

Housing is an expensive immovable property. The general rule of daily life experience indicates that an owner would generally not easily overlook an obvious defect in a purchased property at the time of taking delivery. Appellant Huang Ying repeatedly stated in the first instance that at the time of taking delivery of the property, she had raised a clear written objection in the "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form" regarding the decorative steel beam outside the window. The "Owner's Occupancy Acceptance Form" was evidence kept solely by Appellee Meisheng Real Estate Company, and upon request by the court, Meisheng Real Estate Company refused to produce it. Article 75 of the "Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings" provides: "If there is evidence that a party holds evidence and without justifiable reasons refuses to provide it, and the other party claims that the content of the evidence is unfavorable to the holder of the evidence, it may be presumed that the claim is valid." Accordingly, it may be presumed that Huang Ying's claim that she raised a written objection at the time of taking delivery of the property regarding the steel beam outside the window is valid. The finding of the first instance that Huang Ying did not raise any objection at the time of property handover does not conform to the facts and should be corrected.

This case is a dispute over a pre-sale contract for commercial housing. The "Commercial Housing Sale Contract" signed by both parties is legal and valid. Article 107 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If a party fails to perform its contractual obligations, or performs its contractual obligations in a manner that does not conform to the agreement, it shall bear liability for breach of contract, such as continuing performance, taking remedial measures, or compensating for losses." Because the decorative steel beam affected the visual experience of persons inside the room, Appellant Huang Ying sought an order that Appellee Meisheng Real Estate Company bear the responsibility of moving the decorative crossbeam upward by 55 centimeters. Meisheng Real Estate Company insisted that the steel beam was installed considering the aesthetics and coordination of the entire community, and only after obtaining approval from the relevant government authorities and complying with building codes, and that Huang Ying should consider the interests of the entire community. In the contract signed between Meisheng Real Estate Company and Huang Ying, there was no provision regarding the existence of a decorative steel beam outside the pre-sold property; on the sand table model displayed by Meisheng Real Estate Company to Huang Ying, there was no decorative steel beam outside the model property; yet the property delivered by Meisheng Real Estate Company to Huang Ying had a decorative steel beam obstructing the window. Meisheng Real Estate Company's performance of its contractual obligations did not conform to the agreement, and it should bear liability for breach of contract according to law. Whether the installation of the steel beam underwent administrative approval and complied with building codes pertains to a separate legal relationship and cannot constitute grounds for Meisheng Real Estate Company to be exempted from liability for non-performance or breach of contract. An owner spends a substantial amount of money to purchase a property, focusing not on the aesthetics of the building's exterior walls but on whether the various facilities inside the property are conducive to living and use. It was only under this premise that Huang Ying could have entered into the "Commercial Housing Sale Contract" with Meisheng Real Estate Company. Examining the law and considering the principles of reasonableness, the decorative function of the steel beam cannot be preserved at the expense of sacrificing the contractual purpose that the owner sought to achieve by entering into the "Commercial Housing Sale Contract". Huang Ying's claim to move the decorative crossbeam upward by 55 centimeters is supported by the report of Beijing Capital Engineering Architectural Design Co., Ltd., which demonstrates technical feasibility and can remedy the adverse effects caused by the decorative steel beam at a relatively low cost. This opinion should be adopted.

In summary, the judgment of first instance was based on unclear findings of fact, leading to an inappropriate decision, and should be corrected. Accordingly, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 153(1)(iii) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment on July 8, 2005:

1. Set aside the civil judgment of first instance;

2. Within 10 days after this judgment takes effect, Appellee Meisheng Real Estate Company shall move the decorative steel beam crossbeam outside the window of the property purchased by Appellant Huang Ying upward by 55 centimeters and re-weld it.

Court costs of RMB 50 for each of the first and second instances shall be borne by Appellee Meisheng Real Estate Company.

This judgment is final.
